article_title: Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning
citation: Hayo Reinders and Sorada Wattana. (2015). Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning. ReCALL, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344014000226
title: Willingness to communicate (WTC) as a framework for studying affect in digital game-based language learning
description: The article organises its inquiry around willingness to communicate (WTC) in a second language, adopting the situational model of MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément & Noels (1998). WTC is used as the lens through which the interview data on gameplay experiences are interpreted, connecting affective factors such as lowered anxiety to learners' readiness to interact in English. The article positions WTC alongside claims that games are "motivating" and "lower affective barriers in learning".
requirements: Requires interview or observational data on learners' communicative behaviour in the target language to assess WTC.
constraints: Applied here to five EFL students at a Thai university in a digital game-based learning context.
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate in English as a foreign language
examples: The authors conducted 30 interviews with five students to identify gameplay's impact on their willingness to communicate in English.
key_sources: Hayo Reinders and Sorada Wattana. (2015). Affect and willingness to communicate in digital game-based learning. ReCALL, Volume 27, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344014000226

article_title: Understanding Visitors’ Curiosity in a Science Centre with Deep Question Processing Network
citation: Zhaozhen Xu, Amelia Howarth, Nicole Briggs, Nello Cristianini. (2024). Understanding Visitors' Curiosity in a Science Centre with Deep Question Processing Network. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00377-8
title: WTC corpus of 8,600 curated open-domain questions from We The Curious
description: The WTC corpus is a dataset of open-domain questions collected by the Bristol science centre We The Curious through Project What If between January 2017 and October 2019 via four methods: the Project What If Cube, Curious Cube outings, staff-facilitated question gathering, and online input. After manual moderation and automated pre-processing removing duplicates and questions shorter than three words, "the filtered WTC dataset contains 8,600 questions". The corpus has 5,732 vocabulary items, question lengths of 3-55 words, and an average length of 7.15 words, and is used in this article to demonstrate QBERT's applicability to real-world question data.
requirements: Questions were collected verbatim and moderated by We The Curious staff, with identifying information and inappropriate content removed before analysis.
constraints: The anonymised and moderated WTC dataset is available from We The Curious on reasonable request for research purposes, not released openly; personal data is not shared with other parties, including the analysis team.
target_learners: Science centre visitors and members of the public of all ages and backgrounds in Bristol
target_learning_goals: Understanding community curiosity to inform exhibitions and educational content
examples: Questions collected include "Are all babies born with blue eyes?" and counterfactual questions such as "How long will the earth and humans last if we carry on damaging it and nothing changes?"
key_sources: Zhaozhen Xu, Amelia Howarth, Nicole Briggs, Nello Cristianini. (2024). Understanding Visitors' Curiosity in a Science Centre with Deep Question Processing Network. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00377-8

article_title: The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students
citation: Mohd Nasir Ismail, Nurfaezah Mamat, Adnan Jamaludin. (2018). The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: WTAILS — WebOPAC Training Assessment Information Literacy Skills instrument
description: WTAILS is the multiple-choice posttest instrument used in this study to measure students' information literacy skills. It was "designed to evaluate student learning in four content areas of th e ACRL Information Literacy  Competency Standards for Higher Education," measuring Standard One, Two, Three and Five; Standard Four was excluded because it is "not compatible with a multiple-choice item format." The test must be completed in an hour, with lower-order skills measured by most items and one-third measuring higher-order skills. Its Cronbach's alpha in this study was 0.782.
requirements: Administered as a one-hour multiple-choice test
Items based on ACRL Standards One, Two, Three and Five
constraints: Standard Four of the ACRL standards is not assessed because it requires examination or evaluation of student-produced products rather than multiple-choice items
target_learning_goals: ability to locate, evaluate, and use information effectively
examples: WTAILS served as the dependent-variable posttest across all three instructional method groups (WSTTG, WSTT, T) in the 3x2 factorial study.
key_sources: Mohd Nasir Ismail, Nurfaezah Mamat, Adnan Jamaludin. (2018). The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165734

article_title: Enhancing English Learners' Willingness to Communicate through Debate and Philosophy Inquiry Discussion
citation: Mardziah Shamsudin, Moomala Othman, Maryam Jahedi & Dalia Aralas. (2017). Enhancing English Learners' Willingness to Communicate through Debate and Philosophy Inquiry Discussion. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p145
title: Willingness to Communicate as a construct resting on Communication Apprehension and Self-Communicative Competence
description: The article treats Willingness to Communicate as a psychological precursor of L2 speech, defined as "a readiness to speak in the L2 at a particular time with a specific person". It holds that WTC "is mostly dependent on two elements i.e., Communication Apprehension (CA) and Self-Communicative Competence (CC)": CA is the anxiety learners experience when communicating, while CC is the feeling of confidence one has to communicate effectively in a situation. The study operationalises these with McCroskey's (1992) questionnaire sections and interprets its results through this two-element account.
requirements: Measured with a WTC questionnaire distinguishing WTC, Communication Apprehension, and Communicative Competence sections
constraints: WTC is framed as situation- and interlocutor-specific, varying inside versus outside the classroom
target_learning_goals: willingness to communicate in the target language
examples: The study measured WTC, CA and CC before and after eight weeks of either Debate or PI discussion instruction
key_sources: Mardziah Shamsudin, Moomala Othman, Maryam Jahedi & Dalia Aralas. (2017). Enhancing English Learners' Willingness to Communicate through Debate and Philosophy Inquiry Discussion. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p145

article_title: The Impact of Teaching Communication Strategies on EFL Learners' Willingness to Communicate
citation: Abulfazl Mesgarshahr, Esmaeel Abdollahzadeh. (2014). The impact of teaching communication strategies on EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2014.4.1.4
title: WTC model with Communication Apprehension and Self-perceived Communicative Competence as immediate precursors
description: The article organizes its intervention around the model proposed by MacIntyre (1994), in which Willingness to Communicate is determined by two immediate precursors. It states that "the model specifically focuses on two of the most immediate precursors of WTC: Communication Apprehension, and Self-perceived Communicative Competence." Communication Apprehension is fear or anxiety associated with communication, while Self-perceived Communicative Competence is the perception of one’s own competence, which the article says ultimately determines whether to communicate. The study’s rationale is that CSs raise WTC by reducing apprehension and bolstering perceived competence.
requirements: Learners must perceive themselves as equipped to handle communication problems for perceived competence to rise
constraints: WTC is conceived here as willingness to interact inside the EFL classroom, since in Iran the class is the main place affording communication opportunities
target_learners: EFL learners, pre-intermediate level, adolescents and adults
key_sources: Abulfazl Mesgarshahr, Esmaeel Abdollahzadeh. (2014). The impact of teaching communication strategies on EFL learners’ Willingness to Communicate. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2014.4.1.4
